newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche upbeat despite MGAM charge.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche upbeat despite MGAM charge.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Bank AG said Wednesday it had to pay more than a billion marks ($594 million) to sort out the 1996 mismanagement scandal at its London investment funds unit MGAM.
Conceding that it needed to do more to prove itself a global player in investment banking, the German giant nonetheless downplayed the MGAM saga as a one-time event.
"For 1997 we are confident overall," Chief Executive Hilmar Kopper told a news conference, as he gave his last major address to reporters before his retirement in May.
"We are confident that the strategic decisions and structural changes in the group, which entail considerable preliminary costs, will have an even stronger positive impact in 1997," Kopper added.

Deutsche reported a 37 percent rise in operating profit for 1996 to 5.8 billion marks ($3.44 billion). Its net income rose 4.6 percent to 2.2 billion marks ($1.3 billion), depressed by a surge in tax costs.
Kopper said 1996 was a good year overall, although interest income was pressured by continued low interest rates, and a "highly successful year" for asset management.

But the bank was still forced to set aside between 1.1 billion ($653 million) and 1.2 billion marks ($712 million) to cover damages related to Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, pushing its extraordinary expenses item up to 1.49 billion marks ($589 million) from 377 million marks ($224 million). The expenses were offset by profits from investments of roughly the same amount.
"We don't know yet exactly (what the costs will be), the calculations are still continuing," Kopper said.

The charge stems from the three-day suspension of three mutual funds in September due to irregularities centering on unquoted securities. Peter Young, the portfolio manager responsible for two of the funds, was dismissed and four other managers left the company over the affair.
Deutsche previously estimated that compensating investors would cost about 200 million British pounds ($323.6 million) on top of a net injection into the funds of 180 million pounds ($291.2 million).
Kopper said his optimism for 1997 was based on strong operating income and trading earnings for the first two months. Low interest rates would likely keep lending demand buoyant.
